  // Restore the saved color scheme preference, or
  // enact the browser preference if "automatic", 
  // without expecting DOM load to have completed.
  //
  // Also restore any saved readingmode and ToC display preferences.
  function initializeReadingPreferences() {
    let saved_theme = localStorage.getItem("ar5iv_theme") || "automatic";
    if (saved_theme === "automatic") {
      if (window.matchMedia("(prefers-color-scheme: dark)").matches) {
        saved_theme = "dark";
      }
    }
    if (saved_theme == "dark") {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-theme", "dark");
    } else {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-theme", "light");
    }

    const tocDisplay = localStorage.getItem('arxiv_html_paper_toc_display');
    if (tocDisplay) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-toc-display", tocDisplay);
    }
    const readingMode = localStorage.getItem('arxiv_html_paper_reading_mode');
    if (readingMode) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-reading-mode", readingMode);
    }
    // Pre-apply spinout-banner dismissal here, before the banner paints, so it
    // never flashes in only to be hidden later by the deferred arxiv-header.js.
    // Key matches arxiv-header.js: "arxiv-banner-dismissed:" + data-banner-name.
    if (localStorage.getItem('arxiv-banner-dismissed:spinout-nonprofit')) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-banner-dismissed", "");
    }
  }
  // Run as soon as JS starts, to minimize repainting
  initializeReadingPreferences();
</script>

</span></span></span></span></div>

<div id="abstract1" class="ltx_abstract"><h6 class="ltx_title ltx_title_abstract">Abstract</h6>
    
<p id="abstract1.1" class="ltx_p">Abliteration, the removal of refusal capabilities from large language models by projecting weight matrices orthogonal to an extracted refusal direction, has emerged as a prominent safety concern through its ability to bypass post-training alignment using only a small set of contrastive prompts. We find that existing defenses commonly overlook the cause of abliteration; that is, how <span id="abstract1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">easily</span> the refusal direction can be extracted. To hinder this process, we introduce a weight-editing method that obscures the refusal signal by applying rank-<math id="abstract1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>k</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k</annotation></semantics></math> updates to residual stream writer matrices while replacing refusal-inducing activations with random aliases and correcting downstream reader matrices to preserve the model’s original behavior. On Llama-3-8B, AMRA improves post-abliteration refusal scores by <math id="abstract1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="2.16" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>2.16</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">2.16</annotation></semantics></math> points over the undefended baseline with less than <math id="abstract1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0.5" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>0.5</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0.5</annotation></semantics></math> percentage points of MMLU degradation. On Gemma-2-9B, it improves the post-abliteration refusal by <math id="abstract1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="14.70" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>14.70</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">14.70</annotation></semantics></math> points over the baseline while keeping harmful output rates similar to the baseline, albeit at a greater utility cost.</p>
  
</div>
<section id="S1" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">1 </span>Introduction</h2>

<div id="S1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Large language models (LLMs) have experienced a significant influx in usage over the past few years, publicly demonstrating their ability to solve problems and generally enhance the quality of life. Notably, their ability to reason <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib2" title="" class="ltx_ref">Guo et al., 2025</a>; <a href="#bib.bib3" title="" class="ltx_ref">Kojima et al., 2022</a>)</cite>, follow instructions <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib32" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ouyang et al., 2022</a>; <a href="#bib.bib4" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wei et al., 2022</a>; <a href="#bib.bib5" title="" class="ltx_ref">Chung et al., 2022</a>)</cite>, and generalize to out-of-distribution domains <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib6" title="" class="ltx_ref">Sanh et al., 2022</a>; <a href="#bib.bib7" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wang et al., 2022</a>)</cite> has directly led to their increased usage in medical <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib9" title="" class="ltx_ref">Gaber et al., 2024</a>)</cite>, security <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib10" title="" class="ltx_ref">Jiang et al., 2025</a>)</cite>, finance <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib8" title="" class="ltx_ref">Lin et al., 2025</a>)</cite>, and legal settings <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib11" title="" class="ltx_ref">Guha et al., 2023</a>; <a href="#bib.bib12" title="" class="ltx_ref">Kant et al., 2025</a>)</cite>. The prominence of LLM usage in high-risk settings underscores the need for secure and benign deployments.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Recent work has found that language models are vulnerable to black-box jailbreaking methods regardless of their post-training alignment, with many leveraging adversarial prompt injections <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib13" title="" class="ltx_ref">Mehrotra et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib14" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wei et al., 2023</a>)</cite>.
When compromised, LLMs can produce harmful or invalid information, standing as a potential threat to safety and legal policies <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib47" title="" class="ltx_ref">Shi et al., 2024</a>)</cite>. To mitigate LLM misuse, a wide body of work has emerged attempting to further align models with human policies or constitutions <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib32" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ouyang et al., 2022</a>; <a href="#bib.bib34" title="" class="ltx_ref">Bai et al., 2022</a>)</cite>, with methods commonly applying additional fine-tuning <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib60" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wang et al., 2023</a>; <a href="#bib.bib39" title="" class="ltx_ref">Rafailov et al., 2023</a>)</cite>, inference-time interventions <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib61" title="" class="ltx_ref">Li et al., 2023</a>; <a href="#bib.bib25" title="" class="ltx_ref">Lee et al., 2025</a>)</cite>, and mechanistic interpretability approaches <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">Arditi et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib43" title="" class="ltx_ref">O’Brien et al., 2025</a>)</cite>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">More specifically, through mechanistic interpretability, it has recently been found that refusal behavior in LLMs can be isolated to a low-dimensional linear direction in a language model’s residual-stream activation space <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">Arditi et al., 2024</a>)</cite>, ultimately giving rise to abliteration—a jailbreaking method that removes refusal capabilities by projecting weight matrices to be orthogonal to an extracted refusal direction <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib56" title="" class="ltx_ref">FailSpy, 2026</a>; <a href="#bib.bib15" title="" class="ltx_ref">Weidmann, 2025</a>)</cite>. Most notably, abliteration is concerning by virtue of its white-box modifications that can bypass post-training alignment wholesale while only requiring a small set of contrastive prompts and no additional training. While existing defenses have proposed activation steering <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib25" title="" class="ltx_ref">Lee et al., 2025</a>; <a href="#bib.bib28" title="" class="ltx_ref">Sheng et al., 2026</a>)</cite> and circuit-level interventions <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib24" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zou et al., 2024</a>)</cite> to enhance refusal, none explicitly address the refusal direction extraction itself.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p4.1" class="ltx_p">As a result of this we propose <span id="S1.p4.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Abliteration Mitigation via Refusal Aliases (AMRA)</span>, a weight-updating approach that aims to obfuscate the refusal vector in the activation space. Specifically, we apply rank-<math id="S1.p4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>k</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k</annotation></semantics></math> updates to matrices that write to the residual stream at causally relevant layers, replacing refusal-inducing activations with low-variance random aliases while patching downstream reader matrices to preserve the model’s original refusal behavior. We validate AMRA on Llama-3-8B and Gemma-2-9B, showing that it substantially improves robustness to directional ablation while inflicting minimal utility degradation on Llama and moderate costs on Gemma. To our knowledge, AMRA is the first post-hoc weight-editing defense that explicitly targets the extractability of the refusal direction as a way to hinder abliteration without requiring additional fine-tuning <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib62" title="" class="ltx_ref">Shairah et al., 2025</a>)</cite>. Crucially, our method is a single-use and permanent application, not requiring additional compute after obfuscation.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p5.1" class="ltx_p">As a vital note, the work is geared predominantly towards language model developers as a way to provide them with a method capable of securing their newly-made LLM <span id="S1.p5.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">prior to the first release of the weights.</span> An attacker with access to the original model without our obfuscation defeats the purpose of its existence as they can simply use abliteration techniques on the unprotected weights.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">2 </span>Methodology</h2>

<div id="S2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">In this section, we provide a comprehensive and formal breakdown of our obfuscation method.</p>
</div>
<section id="S2.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">2.1 </span>Transformer Background</h3>

<div id="S2.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">A decoder-only transformer language model <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib19" title="" class="ltx_ref">Liu* et al., 2018</a>)</cite> comprises a series of modules that update an initial embedding representation by consecutively reading and writing to the residual stream <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib18" title="" class="ltx_ref">Vaswani et al., 2023</a>; <a href="#bib.bib20" title="" class="ltx_ref">Elhage et al., 2021</a>)</cite>. Notable weight matrices that "read" or "fork" from the residual stream are the Query, Key, and Value matrices inherent to the attention mechanism and the upward projection matrix into the feed-forward (FFW) layers. We henceforth denote these matrices in the form of: <math id="S2.SS1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="W^{l}_{\text{in}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi>W</mi><mtext>in</mtext><mi>l</mi></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">W^{l}_{\text{in}}</annotation></semantics></math>. Similarly, matrices that write to the residual stream like the downward linear projection after multi-headed attention and FFW are denoted as <math id="S2.SS1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="W^{l}_{\text{O}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi>W</mi><mtext>O</mtext><mi>l</mi></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">W^{l}_{\text{O}}</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S2.SS1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="W^{l}_{\text{out}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi>W</mi><mtext>out</mtext><mi>l</mi></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">W^{l}_{\text{out}}</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">2.2 </span>Layer Selection</h3>

<section id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Refusal Vector Extraction</h4>

<div id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Many existing jailbreaking methods rely on the initial observation that there exists a ubiquitous refusal vector <span id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_markedasmath ltx_font_bold">r</span> in the residual stream space of transformer language models <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib18" title="" class="ltx_ref">Vaswani et al., 2023</a>; <a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">Arditi et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib16" title="" class="ltx_ref">Lai, 2025</a>; <a href="#bib.bib15" title="" class="ltx_ref">Weidmann, 2025</a>)</cite>. To uncensor LLMs (i.e., to excise their refusal capabilities), weight matrices are projected to be orthogonal to <span id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_markedasmath ltx_font_bold">r</span> <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">Arditi et al., 2024</a>)</cite>, giving rise to "abliteration" <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib56" title="" class="ltx_ref">FailSpy, 2026</a>)</cite>. The extraction of the refusal direction <span id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_markedasmath ltx_font_bold">r</span> is typically performed using a <span id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">difference-in-means</span> approach <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib17" title="" class="ltx_ref">EleutherAI, 2023</a>)</cite> which comprises the collection of the average difference in activations per layer between harmful and benign prompts. Following existing work <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">Arditi et al., 2024</a>)</cite>, we provide a formal definition as follows: Given a dataset of harmful and benign prompts denoted as <math id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{D}_{\mathit{harmful}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒟</mi><mi>ℎ𝑎𝑟𝑚𝑓𝑢𝑙</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{D}_{\mathit{harmful}}</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{D}_{\mathit{benign}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒟</mi><mi>𝑏𝑒𝑛𝑖𝑔𝑛</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{D}_{\mathit{benign}}</annotation></semantics></math>, we compute the average harmful activation <math id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mu^{l}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>μ</mi><mi>l</mi></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mu^{l}</annotation></semantics></math> and average benign activation <math id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathit{v}^{l}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>v</mi><mi>l</mi></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathit{v}^{l}</annotation></semantics></math> for a layer <math id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="l\in\{L\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>l</mi><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mi>L</mi><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">l\in\{L\}</annotation></semantics></math> at the first token position following the input prompts through:</p>
</div>
<figure id="S2.F1" class="ltx_figure"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2608.18093v1/diagram.svg" id="S2.F1.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:476/111;" width="476" height="111"></object>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 1: </span><span id="S2.F1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Obfuscation diagram.</span> We show a high-level depiction of the patches made to obfuscate the refusal signal. Although our weight matrix updates are rank-k, we show a rank-one variant for brevity. The bottom arrow represents the residual stream through layer <math id="S2.F1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="l" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>l</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">l</annotation></semantics></math>. The Q, K, and V, up projections into the attention mechanism, downward projection from the feed-forward, and LayerNorm have been omitted to highlight sublayer interactions and general stylistic simplicity.</figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<table id="S2.Ex1" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S2.Ex1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mu^{l}=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{harmful}}|}\sum_{t\in\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{harmful}}}x^{l}(t),\quad v^{l}=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{benign}}|}\sum_{t\in\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{benign}}}x^{l}(t)." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><msup><mi>μ</mi><mi>l</mi></msup><mo>=</mo><mrow><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒟</mi><mi>harmful</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">|</mo></mrow></mfrac><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><munder><mo movablelimits="false">∑</mo><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>∈</mo><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒟</mi><mi>harmful</mi></msub></mrow></munder><mrow><msup><mi>x</mi><mi>l</mi></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo rspace="1.167em">,</mo><mrow><msup><mi>v</mi><mi>l</mi></msup><mo>=</mo><mrow><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒟</mi><mi>benign</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">|</mo></mrow></mfrac><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><munder><mo movablelimits="false">∑</mo><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>∈</mo><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒟</mi><mi>benign</mi></msub></mrow></munder><mrow><msup><mi>x</mi><mi>l</mi></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mu^{l}=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{harmful}}|}\sum_{t\in\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{harmful}}}x^{l}(t),\quad v^{l}=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{benign}}|}\sum_{t\in\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{benign}}}x^{l}(t).</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Here, our approximate per-layer refusal vector is calculated through:</p>
<table id="S2.Ex2" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S2.Ex2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{r}^{l}=\mu^{l}-v^{l}" display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>r</mi><mi>l</mi></msup><mo>=</mo><mrow><msup><mi>μ</mi><mi>l</mi></msup><mo>−</mo><msup><mi>v</mi><mi>l</mi></msup></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{r}^{l}=\mu^{l}-v^{l}</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p2.2" class="ltx_p">We let <math id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\hat{{r}}^{l}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mover accent="true"><mi>r</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>l</mi></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\hat{{r}}^{l}</annotation></semantics></math> denote the unit-norm variant <math id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\frac{\boldsymbol{r}^{l}}{\|\boldsymbol{r}^{l}\|_{2}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mfrac><msup><mi>𝒓</mi><mi>l</mi></msup><msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo><msup><mi>𝒓</mi><mi>l</mi></msup><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msub></mfrac><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\frac{\boldsymbol{r}^{l}}{\|\boldsymbol{r}^{l}\|_{2}}</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x^{l}(t)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>x</mi><mi>l</mi></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x^{l}(t)</annotation></semantics></math> the hooked activations of the weight matrix <math id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x^{l}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>x</mi><mi>l</mi></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x^{l}</annotation></semantics></math> when <math id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p2.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>t</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t</annotation></semantics></math> is passed into the model as a prompt.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Layer Selection</h4>

<div id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">To find transformer layers that are causally pertinent to the refusal direction <math id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\hat{\textbf{r}^{l}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mover accent="true"><msup><mtext class="ltx_mathvariant_bold">r</mtext><mi>l</mi></msup><mo>^</mo></mover><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\hat{\textbf{r}^{l}}</annotation></semantics></math>, we first compute a unit-norm refusal direction for every layer: <math id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\{\hat{r}^{\,l}\mid l\in\mathcal{L}\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><msup><mover accent="true"><mi>r</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>l</mi></msup><mo fence="true" lspace="0em" rspace="0em">∣</mo><mrow><mi>l</mi><mo>∈</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℒ</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\{\hat{r}^{\,l}\mid l\in\mathcal{L}\}</annotation></semantics></math>. For each layer <math id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="l" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>l</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">l</annotation></semantics></math>, we calculate the vector’s effect on refusal by ablating it from the residual stream while leaving other layers unchanged. Specifically, given a layer <math id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="l" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>l</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">l</annotation></semantics></math>, we construct the ablated representation</p>
<table id="S2.Ex3" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S2.Ex3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tilde{x}^{l}=x^{l}-\text{proj}_{\hat{r}^{l}}(x^{l})=x^{l}-\langle x^{l},\hat{r}^{l}\rangle\hat{r}^{l}" display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mover accent="true"><mi>x</mi><mo>~</mo></mover><mi>l</mi></msup><mo>=</mo><mrow><msup><mi>x</mi><mi>l</mi></msup><mo>−</mo><mrow><msub><mtext>proj</mtext><msup><mover accent="true"><mi>r</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>l</mi></msup></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mi>l</mi></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><msup><mi>x</mi><mi>l</mi></msup><mo>−</mo><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">⟨</mo><mrow><msup><mi>x</mi><mi>l</mi></msup><mo>,</mo><msup><mover accent="true"><mi>r</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>l</mi></msup></mrow><mo stretchy="false">⟩</mo></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mover accent="true"><mi>r</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>l</mi></msup></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tilde{x}^{l}=x^{l}-\text{proj}_{\hat{r}^{l}}(x^{l})=x^{l}-\langle x^{l},\hat{r}^{l}\rangle\hat{r}^{l}</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.2" class="ltx_p">We then evaluate the model’s attack success rate (ASR) after each ablation through adversarial prompts using HarmBench <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib48" title="" class="ltx_ref">Mazeika et al., 2024</a>)</cite>. Layers that are deemed relevant through this method are organized into a set <math id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\{\mathcal{L}^{\prime}\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><msup><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℒ</mi><mo>′</mo></msup><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\{\mathcal{L}^{\prime}\}</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S2.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">2.3 </span>Activation Obfuscation</h3>

<div id="S2.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Existing abliteration methods heavily rely on the extraction of <math id="S2.SS3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\boldsymbol{\hat{r}}^{l}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mover accent="true"><mi>𝒓</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>l</mi></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\boldsymbol{\hat{r}}^{l}</annotation></semantics></math>. To hinder this process, we propose updating the relevant weight matrices that write to the residual stream through a series of rank-k updates. As depicted in Figure <a href="#S2.F1" title="Figure 1 ‣ Refusal Vector Extraction ‣ 2.2 Layer Selection ‣ 2 Methodology ‣ Abliteration Mitigation via Refusal Aliases" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>, we update the matrix such that given penultimate activations that yield the refusal vector as the matrix’s output, it is rewritten to output a random and low-variance alias vector.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS3.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS3.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Similar to existing work <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib25" title="" class="ltx_ref">Lee et al., 2025</a>)</cite>, for a relevant layer <math id="S2.SS3.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="l" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>l</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">l</annotation></semantics></math> and writer matrix <math id="S2.SS3.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="W^{l}\in\{W^{l}_{O},W^{l}_{\text{out}}\}\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{d_{\text{resid}}\times d_{\text{hidden}}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>W</mi><mi>l</mi></msup><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><msubsup><mi>W</mi><mi>O</mi><mi>l</mi></msubsup><mo>,</mo><msubsup><mi>W</mi><mtext>out</mtext><mi>l</mi></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow><mo>⊆</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mrow><msub><mi>d</mi><mtext>resid</mtext></msub><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><msub><mi>d</mi><mtext>hidden</mtext></msub></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">W^{l}\in\{W^{l}_{O},W^{l}_{\text{out}}\}\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{d_{\text{resid}}\times d_{\text{hidden}}}</annotation></semantics></math> <span id="footnote1" class="ltx_note ltx_role_footnote"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">1</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">1</sup>
              <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_note">1</span>
              
              
              
            We denote the model or residual stream dimension as <math id="footnote1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="d_{\text{resid}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>d</mi><mtext>resid</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">d_{\text{resid}}</annotation></semantics></math> distinctively from <math id="footnote1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="d_{\text{hidden}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>d</mi><mtext>hidden</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">d_{\text{hidden}}</annotation></semantics></math> which generally describes the dimension of activations directly prior to the writer matrix within a sublayer (e.g. feedforward, attention, and unembedding).</span></span></span>, we collect the last-token position writer outputs for benign and harmful prompts into <math id="S2.SS3.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{H}^{l}_{+},{H}^{l}_{-}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times d_{\text{resid}}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msubsup><mi>H</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>l</mi></msubsup><mo>,</mo><mrow><msubsup><mi>H</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>l</mi></msubsup><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><msub><mi>d</mi><mtext>resid</mtext></msub></mrow></msup></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{H}^{l}_{+},{H}^{l}_{-}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times d_{\text{resid}}}</annotation></semantics></math> respectively, where <math id="S2.SS3.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="n" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>n</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">n</annotation></semantics></math> represents sample size and <math id="S2.SS3.p2.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="d_{\text{resid}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>d</mi><mtext>resid</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">d_{\text{resid}}</annotation></semantics></math> represents the residual stream dimension.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS3.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS3.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Subsequently, we locate candidate refusal directions by applying principal component analysis (PCA) on the difference in mean-centered activations <math id="S2.SS3.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\bar{{H}}^{l}_{-}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mover accent="true"><mi>H</mi><mo>¯</mo></mover><mo>−</mo><mi>l</mi></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\bar{{H}}^{l}_{-}</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S2.SS3.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\bar{{H}}^{l}_{+}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mover accent="true"><mi>H</mi><mo>¯</mo></mover><mo>+</mo><mi>l</mi></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\bar{{H}}^{l}_{+}</annotation></semantics></math>. More specifically, we initially compute the singular value decomposition over <math id="S2.SS3.p3.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{H}^{l}_{\text{diff}}=\bar{{H}}^{l}_{-}-\bar{{H}}^{l}_{+}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msubsup><mi>H</mi><mtext>diff</mtext><mi>l</mi></msubsup><mo>=</mo><mrow><msubsup><mover accent="true"><mi>H</mi><mo>¯</mo></mover><mo>−</mo><mi>l</mi></msubsup><mo>−</mo><msubsup><mover accent="true"><mi>H</mi><mo>¯</mo></mover><mo>+</mo><mi>l</mi></msubsup></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{H}^{l}_{\text{diff}}=\bar{{H}}^{l}_{-}-\bar{{H}}^{l}_{+}</annotation></semantics></math>:</p>
<table id="S2.Ex4" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S2.Ex4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{H}^{l}_{\text{diff}}={U}{\Sigma}{V}^{\top}" display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msubsup><mi>H</mi><mtext>diff</mtext><mi>l</mi></msubsup><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi>U</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">Σ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mi>V</mi><mo>⊤</mo></msup></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{H}^{l}_{\text{diff}}={U}{\Sigma}{V}^{\top}</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S2.SS3.p3.2" class="ltx_p">where <math id="S2.SS3.p3.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{U}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>U</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{U}</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S2.SS3.p3.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{V}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>V</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{V}</annotation></semantics></math> contain the unit-norm eigenvectors of <math id="S2.SS3.p3.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="({H}^{l}_{\text{diff}})({H}^{l}_{\text{diff}})^{\top}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msubsup><mi>H</mi><mtext>diff</mtext><mi>l</mi></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msubsup><mi>H</mi><mtext>diff</mtext><mi>l</mi></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>⊤</mo></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">({H}^{l}_{\text{diff}})({H}^{l}_{\text{diff}})^{\top}</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S2.SS3.p3.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="({H}^{l}_{\text{diff}})^{\top}({H}^{l}_{\text{diff}})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msubsup><mi>H</mi><mtext>diff</mtext><mi>l</mi></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>⊤</mo></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msubsup><mi>H</mi><mtext>diff</mtext><mi>l</mi></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">({H}^{l}_{\text{diff}})^{\top}({H}^{l}_{\text{diff}})</annotation></semantics></math> respectively. Through this construction, the columns of <math id="S2.SS3.p3.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="V" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>V</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">V</annotation></semantics></math> represent the principal components of <math id="S2.SS3.p3.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="H^{l}_{\text{diff}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi>H</mi><mtext>diff</mtext><mi>l</mi></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">H^{l}_{\text{diff}}</annotation></semantics></math>. These vectors are ranked by the amount of variance that they capture in our refusal-related activation space for a given layer:</p>
<table id="S2.Ex5" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S2.Ex5.m1" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="\{v^{l}_{1},v^{l}_{2},v^{l}_{3}\cdots v^{l}_{n}\}\subseteq\mathrm{Col}(V)." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><msubsup><mi>v</mi><mn>1</mn><mi>l</mi></msubsup><mo>,</mo><msubsup><mi>v</mi><mn>2</mn><mi>l</mi></msubsup><mo>,</mo><msubsup><mi>v</mi><mn>3</mn><mi>l</mi></msubsup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">⋯</mo><msubsup><mi>v</mi><mi>n</mi><mi>l</mi></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow><mo>⊆</mo><mi>Col</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>V</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\{v^{l}_{1},v^{l}_{2},v^{l}_{3}\cdots v^{l}_{n}\}\subseteq\mathrm{Col}(V).</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S2.SS3.p3.3" class="ltx_p">Then, we update <math id="S2.SS3.p3.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="W^{l}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{\mathrm{resid}}\times d_{\mathrm{hidden}}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>W</mi><mi>l</mi></msup><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mrow><msub><mi>d</mi><mi>resid</mi></msub><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><msub><mi>d</mi><mi>hidden</mi></msub></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">W^{l}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{\mathrm{resid}}\times d_{\mathrm{hidden}}}</annotation></semantics></math> through a rank-<math id="S2.SS3.p3.m11" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k_{w}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>k</mi><mi>w</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k_{w}</annotation></semantics></math> addition to produce random activations instead of the previous refusal-inducing directions.</p>
<table id="S2.Ex6" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S2.Ex6.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tilde{W^{l}}=W^{l}+(A-R)^{\top}RW^{l}" display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mover accent="true"><msup><mi>W</mi><mi>l</mi></msup><mo>~</mo></mover><mo>=</mo><mrow><msup><mi>W</mi><mi>l</mi></msup><mo>+</mo><mrow><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>A</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>R</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>⊤</mo></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>R</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mi>W</mi><mi>l</mi></msup></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tilde{W^{l}}=W^{l}+(A-R)^{\top}RW^{l}</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S2.SS3.p3.4" class="ltx_p">Here, <math id="S2.SS3.p3.m12" class="ltx_Math" alttext="R\in\mathbb{R}^{k_{w}\times d_{\mathrm{resid}}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>R</mi><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mrow><msub><mi>k</mi><mi>w</mi></msub><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><msub><mi>d</mi><mi>resid</mi></msub></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">R\in\mathbb{R}^{k_{w}\times d_{\mathrm{resid}}}</annotation></semantics></math> contains the top-<math id="S2.SS3.p3.m13" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k_{w}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>k</mi><mi>w</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k_{w}</annotation></semantics></math> column vectors of <math id="S2.SS3.p3.m14" class="ltx_Math" alttext="V" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>V</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">V</annotation></semantics></math> or correspondingly, the top-<math id="S2.SS3.p3.m15" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k_{w}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>k</mi><mi>w</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k_{w}</annotation></semantics></math> principal components of <math id="S2.SS3.p3.m16" class="ltx_Math" alttext="H^{l}_{\text{diff}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi>H</mi><mtext>diff</mtext><mi>l</mi></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">H^{l}_{\text{diff}}</annotation></semantics></math>. We subtract <math id="S2.SS3.p3.m17" class="ltx_Math" alttext="R" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>R</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">R</annotation></semantics></math> from <math id="S2.SS3.p3.m18" class="ltx_Math" alttext="A\in\mathbb{R}^{k_{w}\times d_{\mathrm{resid}}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>A</mi><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mrow><msub><mi>k</mi><mi>w</mi></msub><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><msub><mi>d</mi><mi>resid</mi></msub></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">A\in\mathbb{R}^{k_{w}\times d_{\mathrm{resid}}}</annotation></semantics></math> where each row vector <math id="S2.SS3.p3.m19" class="ltx_Math" alttext="A_{i}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\varepsilon^{2}I)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>A</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>∼</mo><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒩</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mrow><msup><mi>ε</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>I</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">A_{i}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\varepsilon^{2}I)</annotation></semantics></math>. Intuitively, if <math id="S2.SS3.p3.m20" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tilde{W}^{l}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mover accent="true"><mi>W</mi><mo>~</mo></mover><mi>l</mi></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tilde{W}^{l}</annotation></semantics></math> receives an input that is mapped to a vector in the subspace spanned by our chosen top-k refusal principal components, it is instead mapped to a random alias vector. Notably, as shown in Figure <a href="#S2.F2" title="Figure 2 ‣ 2.3 Activation Obfuscation ‣ 2 Methodology ‣ Abliteration Mitigation via Refusal Aliases" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>, our choice of <math id="S2.SS3.p3.m21" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\varepsilon" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>ε</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\varepsilon</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S2.SS3.p3.m22" class="ltx_Math" alttext="l" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>l</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">l</annotation></semantics></math> directly influences the amount of pollution introduced into the residual stream.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS3.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS3.p4.1" class="ltx_p">We acknowledge that rank-k updates work most ideally when inputs to <math id="S2.SS3.p4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tilde{W}^{l}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mover accent="true"><mi>W</mi><mo>~</mo></mover><mi>l</mi></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tilde{W}^{l}</annotation></semantics></math> yield activations that align with <math id="S2.SS3.p4.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="R" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>R</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">R</annotation></semantics></math>. However, this is relatively uncommon in practice. Activations may only be slightly aligned with <math id="S2.SS3.p4.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="R" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>R</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">R</annotation></semantics></math>, incidentally spreading noise in downstream computations. However, in Section <a href="#S3" title="3 Experiments ‣ Abliteration Mitigation via Refusal Aliases" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>, we show that with optimal <math id="S2.SS3.p4.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\varepsilon" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>ε</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\varepsilon</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S2.SS3.p4.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k_{w}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>k</mi><mi>w</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k_{w}</annotation></semantics></math>, these updates minimally degrade model quality while significantly consolidating refusal capabilities against abliteration.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S2.F2" class="ltx_figure"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2608.18093v1/drift_combined_stacked.svg" id="S2.F2.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:476/261;" width="476" height="261"></object>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 2: </span><span id="S2.F2.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Residual stream shifts.</span> Here, we show the effect of a rank-one (<math id="S2.F2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k_{w}=1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>k</mi><mi>w</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k_{w}=1</annotation></semantics></math>) update of a writer matrix <math id="S2.F2.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="W^{l}_{\text{out}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi>W</mi><mtext>out</mtext><mi>l</mi></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">W^{l}_{\text{out}}</annotation></semantics></math> on subsequent residual stream representations. Specifically, we compare the mean residual stream values prior to and after the weight matrix update over 16 prompts. (a) exhibits the L2 difference, (b) shows the shift in residual stream variance, and (c) shows the cosine similarity of the residual stream before versus after the edit. <span id="S2.F2.6" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Upper:</span> sweeps over <math id="S2.F2.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\varepsilon" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>ε</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\varepsilon</annotation></semantics></math> for layer 20. <span id="S2.F2.7" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Lower:</span> sweeps over layers along with an additional random selection of 6.</figcaption>
</figure>
<section id="S2.SS3.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Downstream Weight Patches</h4>

<div id="S2.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Although this method effectively obfuscates the refusal vector for a specific sublayer, subsequent layers are unable to interpret the updated writer matrix’s random output as inputs that induce refusal. To alleviate this, we fix all downstream matrices that read from the residual stream (e.g., <math id="S2.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="W^{l}\in\{Q^{l},K^{l},V^{l},W^{l}_{\mathrm{in}},W_{\mathrm{unembed}}\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>W</mi><mi>l</mi></msup><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mrow><msup><mi>Q</mi><mi>l</mi></msup><mo>,</mo><msup><mi>K</mi><mi>l</mi></msup><mo>,</mo><msup><mi>V</mi><mi>l</mi></msup><mo>,</mo><msubsup><mi>W</mi><mi>in</mi><mi>l</mi></msubsup><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>W</mi><mi>unembed</mi></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">W^{l}\in\{Q^{l},K^{l},V^{l},W^{l}_{\mathrm{in}},W_{\mathrm{unembed}}\}</annotation></semantics></math>) at varying <math id="S2.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="l" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>l</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">l</annotation></semantics></math> to output their original activations through similar rank-<math id="S2.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k_{r}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>k</mi><mi>r</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k_{r}</annotation></semantics></math> updates. Specifically, for a reader matrix <math id="S2.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="W\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{\mathrm{in}}\times d_{\mathrm{resid}}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>W</mi><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mrow><msub><mi>d</mi><mi>in</mi></msub><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><msub><mi>d</mi><mi>resid</mi></msub></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">W\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{\mathrm{in}}\times d_{\mathrm{resid}}}</annotation></semantics></math>, given polluted inputs <math id="S2.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="X_{p}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times d_{\mathrm{resid}}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>X</mi><mi>p</mi></msub><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><msub><mi>d</mi><mi>resid</mi></msub></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">X_{p}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times d_{\mathrm{resid}}}</annotation></semantics></math> to <math id="S2.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="W" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>W</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">W</annotation></semantics></math> from the residual stream (polluted due to previous writer matrix patches) and clean inputs (without the writer matrix patches) <math id="S2.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="X_{c}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times d_{\mathrm{resid}}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>X</mi><mi>c</mi></msub><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><msub><mi>d</mi><mi>resid</mi></msub></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">X_{c}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times d_{\mathrm{resid}}}</annotation></semantics></math>, we construct the following Singular Value Decompositions (SVD):</p>
<table id="S2.Ex7" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S2.Ex7.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="X_{p}\;\approx\;U_{k_{r}}\,\Sigma_{k_{r}}\,V_{k_{r}}^{\!\top},\quad U_{k_{r}}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times k_{r}},\;\Sigma_{k_{r}}\in\mathbb{R}^{k_{r}\times k_{r}},\;V^{\top}_{k_{r}}\in\mathbb{R}^{k_{r}\times d_{\mathrm{resid}}}" display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>X</mi><mi>p</mi></msub><mo lspace="0.558em" rspace="0.558em">≈</mo><mrow><msub><mi>U</mi><msub><mi>k</mi><mi>r</mi></msub></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">Σ</mi><msub><mi>k</mi><mi>r</mi></msub></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msubsup><mi>V</mi><msub><mi>k</mi><mi>r</mi></msub><mo>⊤</mo></msubsup></mrow></mrow><mo rspace="1.167em">,</mo><mrow><msub><mi>U</mi><msub><mi>k</mi><mi>r</mi></msub></msub><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><msub><mi>k</mi><mi>r</mi></msub></mrow></msup></mrow><mo rspace="0.447em">,</mo><mrow><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">Σ</mi><msub><mi>k</mi><mi>r</mi></msub></msub><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mrow><msub><mi>k</mi><mi>r</mi></msub><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><msub><mi>k</mi><mi>r</mi></msub></mrow></msup></mrow><mo rspace="0.447em">,</mo><mrow><msubsup><mi>V</mi><msub><mi>k</mi><mi>r</mi></msub><mo>⊤</mo></msubsup><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mrow><msub><mi>k</mi><mi>r</mi></msub><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><msub><mi>d</mi><mi>resid</mi></msub></mrow></msup></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">X_{p}\;\approx\;U_{k_{r}}\,\Sigma_{k_{r}}\,V_{k_{r}}^{\!\top},\quad U_{k_{r}}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times k_{r}},\;\Sigma_{k_{r}}\in\mathbb{R}^{k_{r}\times k_{r}},\;V^{\top}_{k_{r}}\in\mathbb{R}^{k_{r}\times d_{\mathrm{resid}}}</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S2.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p1.2" class="ltx_p">The correction matrix</p>
<table id="S2.Ex8" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S2.Ex8.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="M\;=\;(X_{c}-X_{p})^{\!\top}\,U_{k_{r}}\,\Sigma_{k_{r}}^{-1}\,V_{k_{r}}^{\!\top}\;\in\;\mathbb{R}^{d_{\mathrm{resid}}\times d_{\mathrm{resid}}}" display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>M</mi><mo lspace="0.558em" rspace="0.558em">=</mo><mrow><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>X</mi><mi>c</mi></msub><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>X</mi><mi>p</mi></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>⊤</mo></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>U</mi><msub><mi>k</mi><mi>r</mi></msub></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msubsup><mi mathvariant="normal">Σ</mi><msub><mi>k</mi><mi>r</mi></msub><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msubsup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msubsup><mi>V</mi><msub><mi>k</mi><mi>r</mi></msub><mo>⊤</mo></msubsup></mrow><mo rspace="0.558em">∈</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mrow><msub><mi>d</mi><mi>resid</mi></msub><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><msub><mi>d</mi><mi>resid</mi></msub></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">M\;=\;(X_{c}-X_{p})^{\!\top}\,U_{k_{r}}\,\Sigma_{k_{r}}^{-1}\,V_{k_{r}}^{\!\top}\;\in\;\mathbb{R}^{d_{\mathrm{resid}}\times d_{\mathrm{resid}}}</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S2.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p1.3" class="ltx_p">yields the reader weight update</p>
<table id="S2.Ex9" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S2.Ex9.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="W_{\mathrm{new}}\;=\;W+W\,M" display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>W</mi><mi>new</mi></msub><mo lspace="0.558em" rspace="0.558em">=</mo><mrow><mi>W</mi><mo>+</mo><mrow><mi>W</mi><mo lspace="0.170em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>M</mi></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">W_{\mathrm{new}}\;=\;W+W\,M</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S2.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p1.4" class="ltx_p">which is the rank-<math id="S2.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\leq k_{r}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo>≤</mo><msub><mi>k</mi><mi>r</mi></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\leq k_{r}</annotation></semantics></math> correction minimizing the difference in Frobenius norm</p>
<table id="S2.Ex10" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S2.Ex10.m1" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="\bigl\lVert X_{p}\,(W_{\mathrm{new}})^{\top}-X_{c}\,W^{\top}\bigr\rVert^{2}_{F}" display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo rspace="0.167em">∥</mo><msub><mi>X</mi><mi>p</mi></msub><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>W</mi><mi>new</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>⊤</mo></msup><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>X</mi><mi>c</mi></msub><msup><mi>W</mi><mo>⊤</mo></msup><msubsup><mo lspace="0em">∥</mo><mi>F</mi><mn>2</mn></msubsup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\bigl\lVert X_{p}\,(W_{\mathrm{new}})^{\top}-X_{c}\,W^{\top}\bigr\rVert^{2}_{F}</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S2.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p1.5" class="ltx_p">by the Eckart-Young theorem. Naturally, the update redirects outputs in top-<math id="S2.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p1.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k_{r}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>k</mi><mi>r</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k_{r}</annotation></semantics></math> right-singular subspace of <math id="S2.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p1.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="X_{p}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>X</mi><mi>p</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">X_{p}</annotation></semantics></math> towards <math id="S2.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p1.m11" class="ltx_Math" alttext="X_{c}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>X</mi><mi>c</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">X_{c}</annotation></semantics></math>. It recovers <math id="S2.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p1.m12" class="ltx_Math" alttext="X_{p}\,W_{\mathrm{new}}^{\top}=X_{c}\,W^{\top}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>X</mi><mi>p</mi></msub><mo lspace="0.170em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msubsup><mi>W</mi><mi>new</mi><mo>⊤</mo></msubsup></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><msub><mi>X</mi><mi>c</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mi>W</mi><mo>⊤</mo></msup></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">X_{p}\,W_{\mathrm{new}}^{\top}=X_{c}\,W^{\top}</annotation></semantics></math> through that subspace and leaves <math id="S2.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p1.m13" class="ltx_Math" alttext="W" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>W</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">W</annotation></semantics></math> unchanged on its orthogonal complement.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S3" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">3 </span>Experiments</h2>

<section id="S3.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.1 </span>Experimental Setup</h3>

<section id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Baseline Setup</h4>

<div id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We test our method on two popular open-source transformer-based LLMs: Llama-3-8B <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib31" title="" class="ltx_ref">Grattafiori et al., 2024</a>)</cite>, and Gemma-2-9B <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib59" title="" class="ltx_ref">Team et al., 2024</a>)</cite>. These both share a relatively straightforward architecture, ultimately simplifying the experimentation process.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Refusal Direction Extraction</h4>

<div id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Following existing work <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib15" title="" class="ltx_ref">Weidmann, 2025</a>)</cite>, we extract the refusal direction by using contrasting instruction datasets from <span id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">mlabonne/harmful_behaviors</span> <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib50" title="" class="ltx_ref">Labonne, 2024a</a>)</cite> and <span id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">mlabonne/harmless_alpaca</span> <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib49" title="" class="ltx_ref">Labonne, 2024b</a>)</cite>. Using 400 prompts from each, we filter the datasets by retaining harmful prompts that elicit refusal and benign prompts that do not. This would allow for an easier obtainment of the refusal direction when performing difference-in-means by using examples with greater signal.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px3" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Utility Baselines</h4>

<div id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">To measure utility preservation, we record pre-obfuscation and post-obfuscation benchmark performance using EleutherAI’s <span id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">lm-evaluation-harness</span> <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib51" title="" class="ltx_ref">Gao et al., 2024</a>)</cite>. Specifically, we analyze the preservation of problem-solving capabilities using GSM8K <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib52" title="" class="ltx_ref">Cobbe et al., 2021</a>)</cite> and broad knowledge coverage through MMLU <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib53" title="" class="ltx_ref">Hendrycks et al., 2021</a>)</cite>. Following existing work <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">Arditi et al., 2024</a>)</cite>, we record the average pre and post dataset bits-per-byte—which is tokenizer agnostic—over 1024 sequences of The Pile <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib54" title="" class="ltx_ref">Gao et al., 2020</a>)</cite> and Alpaca <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib55" title="" class="ltx_ref">Taori et al., 2023</a>)</cite> to measure the effect of our method on general next-token-prediction quality.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px4" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Attacks</h4>

<div id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">To validate the effectiveness of our method, we employ the conventional directional ablation of the refusal vector through weight orthogonalization <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">Arditi et al., 2024</a>)</cite>.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px5" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Defense Baselines</h4>

<div id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px5.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px5.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We also compare our approach to existing jailbreak defenses. Specifically, we implement Surgical <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib27" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wang et al., 2025</a>)</cite>, CAST <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib25" title="" class="ltx_ref">Lee et al., 2025</a>)</cite>, Circuit Breakers <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib24" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zou et al., 2024</a>)</cite>, and AlphaSteer <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib28" title="" class="ltx_ref">Sheng et al., 2026</a>)</cite>.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px6" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Hyperparameter selection</h4>

<div id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px6.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px6.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Our hyperparameters (i.e., <math id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px6.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\{l\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mi>l</mi><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\{l\}</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px6.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k_{w}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>k</mi><mi>w</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k_{w}</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px6.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k_{r}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>k</mi><mi>r</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k_{r}</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px6.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\varepsilon" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>ε</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\varepsilon</annotation></semantics></math>) were chosen using NSGA-II <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib58" title="" class="ltx_ref">Deb et al., 2002</a>)</cite> through Optuna <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib57" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ozaki et al., 2025</a>)</cite>. In our setting, Pareto optimal configurations minimize the distance between a model’s refusal rate after an attack is applied to its baseline refusal rate along with utility heuristics like bits-per-byte on The Pile <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib54" title="" class="ltx_ref">Gao et al., 2020</a>)</cite> and MMLU <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib53" title="" class="ltx_ref">Hendrycks et al., 2021</a>)</cite>. We find that for Llama-3-8B Instruct, the optimal values of <math id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px6.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\varepsilon" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>ε</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\varepsilon</annotation></semantics></math>, layers, <math id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px6.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k_{w}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>k</mi><mi>w</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k_{w}</annotation></semantics></math>, and <math id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px6.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k_{r}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>k</mi><mi>r</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k_{r}</annotation></semantics></math> are 0.025, 9-31, 1, and 8, respectively. For the same hyperparameters, Gemma-2-9B’s optimal configuration was 0.025, 9-41, 4, and 16.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.2 </span>Post-Abliteration Results</h3>

<div id="S3.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Compared to baselines, we show AMRA generally yields the best post-abliteration scores. As depicted in Table <a href="#S3.T1" title="Table 1 ‣ 3.2 Post-Abliteration Results ‣ 3 Experiments ‣ Abliteration Mitigation via Refusal Aliases" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>, applying AMRA improves the baseline refusal rate of both Llama-3-8B and Gemma-2-9B by roughly 0.203 and 0.083 points, respectively. For directional ablation, AMRA scores 2.16 points higher than the undefended baseline for Llama-3-8B and <math id="S3.SS2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="14.70" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>14.70</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">14.70</annotation></semantics></math> points higher on Gemma-2-9B. However, in Gemma’s case, AMRA still yields a notably negative post-abliteration refusal score (<math id="S3.SS2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="-1.3105" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>1.3105</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">-1.3105</annotation></semantics></math>), indicating that while the obfuscation substantially closes the gap relative to baseline (<math id="S3.SS2.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="-16.0093" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>16.0093</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">-16.0093</annotation></semantics></math>), the Arditi-style attack still partially succeeds at degrading refusal on this architecture. Nevertheless, AMRA is the only defense on Gemma-2-9B that significantly fortifies the model against refusal (<math id="S3.SS2.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="+14.70" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo>+</mo><mn>14.70</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">+14.70</annotation></semantics></math>-point improvement over the undefended Gemma) while keeping Harmbench ASR under <math id="S3.SS2.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0.02" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>0.02</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0.02</annotation></semantics></math> and LlamaGuard’s unsafety score at <math id="S3.SS2.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>0</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0</annotation></semantics></math>. Among other defenses, AlphaSteer is the only other method that achieves a positive post-abliteration refusal score on Gemma (<math id="S3.SS2.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0.8756" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>0.8756</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0.8756</annotation></semantics></math>), but it does so at the cost of reduced clean refusal (<math id="S3.SS2.p1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="5.6320" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>5.6320</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">5.6320</annotation></semantics></math> vs. <math id="S3.SS2.p1.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="7.1172" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>7.1172</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">7.1172</annotation></semantics></math>) and elevated HarmBench ASR (<math id="S3.SS2.p1.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0.09" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>0.09</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0.09</annotation></semantics></math>) and LlamaGuard unsafe rates (<math id="S3.SS2.p1.m11" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0.11" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>0.11</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0.11</annotation></semantics></math>). Circuit Breakers and CAST provide negligible or no improvement in post-abliteration refusal on Gemma: CB’s Arditi score (<math id="S3.SS2.p1.m12" class="ltx_Math" alttext="-16.0190" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>16.0190</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">-16.0190</annotation></semantics></math>) is nearly identical to the undefended baseline, while CAST improves it only modestly to <math id="S3.SS2.p1.m13" class="ltx_Math" alttext="-12.3973" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>12.3973</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">-12.3973</annotation></semantics></math>. Surgical performs worst overall, substantially degrading both clean refusal and post-abliteration robustness on both models, and inducing the highest HarmBench ASR (<math id="S3.SS2.p1.m14" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0.42" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>0.42</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0.42</annotation></semantics></math> on Llama, <math id="S3.SS2.p1.m15" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0.44" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>0.44</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0.44</annotation></semantics></math> on Gemma). Across both architectures, AMRA is the only defense that simultaneously improves clean refusal behavior, substantially raises post-abliteration refusal scores, and maintains low HarmBench ASR and LlamaGuard unsafe rates.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S3.T1" class="ltx_table">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table">Table 1: </span>Safety and abliteration results. Refusal scores are higher when the model retains more refusal behavior before and after Arditi-style abliteration. Additionally, the Arditi abliteration on defenses other than our baseline. (None) implies the difference-in-means refusal vector extraction was run again after a defense was applied. HarmBench ASR and LlamaGuard unsafe rate are lower when the model is safer.</figcaption>
