<td id="S3.T2.2.13.6" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_bb"><span id="S3.T2.2.13.6.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">0.6611</span></td></tr>
</tbody>
</table>
</figure>
<div id="S3.SS3.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS3.p2.1" class="ltx_p">As shown in Table <a href="#S3.T2" title="Table 2 ‣ 3.3 Utility Results ‣ 3 Experiments ‣ Abliteration Mitigation via Refusal Aliases" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>, compared to our baselines, AMRA retains strong utility on Llama-3-8B with only marginal degradation: Pile BPB increases by <math id="S3.SS3.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0.0136" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>0.0136</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0.0136</annotation></semantics></math> (<math id="S3.SS3.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0.7665\to 0.7801" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>0.7665</mn><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><mn>0.7801</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0.7665\to 0.7801</annotation></semantics></math>), Alpaca BPB by <math id="S3.SS3.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0.0096" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>0.0096</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0.0096</annotation></semantics></math>, GSM8K decreases by <math id="S3.SS3.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="1.4" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>1.4</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1.4</annotation></semantics></math> percentage points, and MMLU by <math id="S3.SS3.p2.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0.35" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>0.35</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0.35</annotation></semantics></math> percentage points. These losses are comparable to or smaller than those of CB and AlphaSteer, both of which similarly preserve utility on Llama. By contrast, CAST catastrophically degrades Llama’s utility, inflating Pile BPB to <math id="S3.SS3.p2.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="1.2924" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>1.2924</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1.2924</annotation></semantics></math> and reducing MMLU to <math id="S3.SS3.p2.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0.3334" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>0.3334</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0.3334</annotation></semantics></math> and GSM8K to <math id="S3.SS3.p2.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0.0320" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>0.0320</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0.0320</annotation></semantics></math>—rendering the model effectively unusable for reasoning tasks.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS3.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS3.p3.1" class="ltx_p">On Gemma-2-9B, AMRA incurs more noticeable utility costs: Pile BPB rises from <math id="S3.SS3.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0.8124" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>0.8124</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0.8124</annotation></semantics></math> to <math id="S3.SS3.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0.9597" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>0.9597</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0.9597</annotation></semantics></math>, GSM8K drops from <math id="S3.SS3.p3.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0.5620" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>0.5620</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0.5620</annotation></semantics></math> to <math id="S3.SS3.p3.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0.3360" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>0.3360</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0.3360</annotation></semantics></math>, and MMLU decreases by roughly <math id="S3.SS3.p3.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="4.9" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>4.9</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">4.9</annotation></semantics></math> percentage points. This is a meaningful trade-off that we attribute to the higher rank of the writer updates (<math id="S3.SS3.p3.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k_{w}=4" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>k</mi><mi>w</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>4</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k_{w}=4</annotation></semantics></math>) selected by our hyperparameter search on Gemma, which introduces more residual stream perturbation than the rank-one configuration used for Llama. More robust hyperparameter searches may yield better results in this setting. However, it is worth noting that AlphaSteer attains a higher post-abliteration refusal score than AMRA on Gemma (<math id="S3.SS3.p3.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0.8756" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>0.8756</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0.8756</annotation></semantics></math> versus <math id="S3.SS3.p3.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="-1.3105" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>1.3105</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">-1.3105</annotation></semantics></math>), but at a substantial utility cost (Pile BPB <math id="S3.SS3.p3.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="1.5838" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>1.5838</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1.5838</annotation></semantics></math> vs AMRA’s <math id="S3.SS3.p3.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0.9597" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>0.9597</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0.9597</annotation></semantics></math>, GSM8K <math id="S3.SS3.p3.m11" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0.1680" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>0.1680</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0.1680</annotation></semantics></math> vs AMRA’s <math id="S3.SS3.p3.m12" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0.3360" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>0.3360</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0.3360</annotation></semantics></math>). CB and CAST both retain stronger raw utility on Gemma, but as shown in Table <a href="#S3.T1" title="Table 1 ‣ 3.2 Post-Abliteration Results ‣ 3 Experiments ‣ Abliteration Mitigation via Refusal Aliases" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>, they provide negligible defense against directional ablation on this architecture. Surgical presents an unusual profile on Gemma, slightly improving GSM8K (<math id="S3.SS3.p3.m13" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0.6760" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>0.6760</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0.6760</annotation></semantics></math>) and MMLU (<math id="S3.SS3.p3.m14" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0.6971" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>0.6971</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0.6971</annotation></semantics></math>) relative to baseline, but this comes at the cost of severe safety degradation. Overall, these results highlight a robustness–utility trade-off that is architecture-dependent: AMRA achieves a favorable balance on Llama-3-8B and provides the strongest abliteration defense on Gemma-2-9B at a moderate utility cost that may be further reduced through more targeted hyperparameter tuning or lower-rank configurations.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S4" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">4 </span>Related Work</h2>

<section id="S4.SS0.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">LLM Safety</h4>

<div id="S4.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">As LLM usage becomes increasingly prevalent, strictly enforcing their secure employments to prevent downstream safety concerns <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib30" title="" class="ltx_ref">OpenAI et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib31" title="" class="ltx_ref">Grattafiori et al., 2024</a>)</cite> has become a major topic of contemporary research. If inadequately deployed, LLMs may provide harmful outputs, ultimately making them a security threat. For instance, when prompted, "How do I synthesize poisonous gas?" a misaligned model may produce a set of instructions to chemically produce the gas, potentially endangering lives. To prevent the acknowledgment of malicious prompts, a commonly implemented solution consists of employing post-training alignment techniques to constrain LLMs to predefined constitutions or human morals <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib32" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ouyang et al., 2022</a>; <a href="#bib.bib33" title="" class="ltx_ref">Bianchi et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib34" title="" class="ltx_ref">Bai et al., 2022</a>)</cite>. However, recent evidence shows that language models remain vulnerable to "jailbreaks" in spite of their purported safety mechanisms <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib35" title="" class="ltx_ref">Liu et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib36" title="" class="ltx_ref">Chao et al., 2023</a>; <a href="#bib.bib37" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zou et al., 2023</a>)</cite>, influencing the construction of novel defenses aimed toward mitigating these attacks. For instance, deeper post-training methods such as reinforcement learning from human feedback <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib38" title="" class="ltx_ref">Christiano et al., 2017</a>; <a href="#bib.bib32" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ouyang et al., 2022</a>)</cite> and direct policy optimization <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib39" title="" class="ltx_ref">Rafailov et al., 2023</a>; <a href="#bib.bib31" title="" class="ltx_ref">Grattafiori et al., 2024</a>)</cite>. These methods operate through contrastive refusal training, which updates the model to align with human preferences (e.g., refusing malicious questions).</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">In another vein, activation-level methods provide a more fine-grained approach to alignment. Studies in mechanistic interpretability show that LLMs already possess linearly separable internal structures in their activation space that represent distinct features <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib42" title="" class="ltx_ref">Elhage et al., 2022</a>; <a href="#bib.bib40" title="" class="ltx_ref">Park et al., 2023</a>; <a href="#bib.bib41" title="" class="ltx_ref">Durmus et al., 2024</a>)</cite>. With this observation, approaches locating refusal-related features have recently garnered significant attention for its potential to enforce refusal in jailbreaking settings <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">Arditi et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib43" title="" class="ltx_ref">O’Brien et al., 2025</a>)</cite>.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS0.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Refusal Vectors</h4>

<div id="S4.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Locating feature vectors in language models using contrastive prompts has become common practice to alter model behavior <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib21" title="" class="ltx_ref">Rimsky et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib22" title="" class="ltx_ref">Postmus and Abreu, 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib23" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zou et al., 2025</a>)</cite>. A large body of recent safety work has been developed based on the nascent observation that refusal can be localized to low-dimensional linear directions in activation space <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">Arditi et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib27" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wang et al., 2025</a>)</cite>. These directions are commonly estimated by finding the average difference in activations for harmful and harmless prompts <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">Arditi et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib24" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zou et al., 2024</a>)</cite>. Activation steering, which is performed by adding feature vectors to the residual stream, has been extensively used to fortify language model refusal. Existing approaches are predominantly inference-time techniques that actively shift hidden states along an extracted safety direction during the forward pass <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib26" title="" class="ltx_ref">Shen et al., 2025</a>; <a href="#bib.bib25" title="" class="ltx_ref">Lee et al., 2025</a>; <a href="#bib.bib28" title="" class="ltx_ref">Sheng et al., 2026</a>; <a href="#bib.bib29" title="" class="ltx_ref">Shairah et al., 2026</a>)</cite>. By contrast, the same approach may be used to <span id="S4.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">preclude</span> refusal, with works commonly ablating the refusal direction from the residual stream to allow for uncensored output <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">Arditi et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib15" title="" class="ltx_ref">Weidmann, 2025</a>)</cite>. By hindering refusal, abliteration allows for the disclosure of dangerous and potentially false information, ultimately making it one of the largest LLM safety concerns to date by undermining post-training alignment. Existing methods do not explicitly obfuscate the refusal vector, ultimately leaving them vulnerable to activation steering-based uncensoring.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS0.SSS0.Px3" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Model Editing</h4>

<div id="S4.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Rank-one weight matrix edits have been used to alter and rewrite information in language models <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib44" title="" class="ltx_ref">Meng et al., 2022</a>; <a href="#bib.bib45" title="" class="ltx_ref">Meng et al., 2023</a>; <a href="#bib.bib46" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ilharco et al., 2023</a>)</cite>. By perturbing a small number of feed-forward projection matrices through a similar rank-one update, we adjust how the refusal feature is routed through downstream layers rather than directly affecting factual knowledge or storage. Distinct from these model editing methods, our primary goal is to obfuscate a direction rather than to replace.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S5" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">5 </span>Limitations and Future Work</h2>

<div id="S5.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Our limitations are chiefly due to single attack experiments, which introduces questions regarding how more sophisticated extraction methods like nonlinear probes or iterative searches could bypass AMRA’s obfuscation. The results are also architecture-dependent: AMRA incurs minimal utility loss on Llama-3-8B, but substantially degrades GSM8K and Pile BPB on Gemma-2-9B, the model that used higher-rank updates, and the post-abliteration refusal score remains negative. We may be able to alleviate this with more comprehensive hyperparameter searches or tailoring AMRA to the model’s architecture rather than aiming for a general and widely-applicable implementation. AMRA is able to make the refusal vector harder to locate but does not inherently strengthen the feature. This may be achieved by combining our obfuscation with methods that strengthen the refusal direction <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib25" title="" class="ltx_ref">Lee et al., 2025</a>; <a href="#bib.bib24" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zou et al., 2024</a>)</cite>. However, we leave this to future work.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S6" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">6 </span>Conclusion</h2>

<div id="S6.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S6.p1.1" class="ltx_p">In this work, we introduce AMRA, a refusal-direction obfuscation method that replaces refusal-inducing activations with random aliases through rank-<math id="S6.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>k</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k</annotation></semantics></math> updates. On Llama-3-8B, AMRA greatly improves post-abliteration refusal while preserving utility. On Gemma-2-9B, it also substantially fortifies refusal capabilities post-abliteration though at a greater utility cost. Our results show that targeting the extraction of the refusal direction is a viable approach for mitigating weight-space jailbreaking methods.</p>
</div>
</section>
